dataguide_desc_speed: Velocidad actual del vehículo en las unidades seleccionadas.
dataguide_desc_gear: Marcha actual (0 = marcha atrás; 1–n = marchas hacia delante).
dataguide_desc_throttle_brake: Entrada del pedal como porcentaje de su recorrido total (0–100 %).
dataguide_desc_steer: Ángulo del volante en grados, ajustado según el bloqueo de dirección configurado.
dataguide_desc_boost: Presión de sobrealimentación del turbo o compresor, en PSI por encima de la presión atmosférica.
dataguide_desc_power_torque: Potencia del motor a las RPM actuales.
dataguide_desc_fuel: % consumido desde el inicio de la vuelta · % restante en el depósito.
dataguide_desc_balance: Detector híbrido de subviraje y sobreviraje. Combina dos señales físicas independientes: tasa de guiñada frente a curvatura de la trayectoria (ω comparada con Aᵧ/V, estándar MoTeC/VBox) y diferencia del ángulo de deslizamiento entre ejes delantero y trasero. + = subviraje (las ruedas delanteras se desvían más que las traseras) · − = sobreviraje (la carrocería gira más que la trayectoria). Solo se activa con |latG| ≥ 0.25g, por lo que el patinaje o bloqueo en línea recta nunca cuenta como desequilibrio.
dataguide_desc_g_force: Fuerzas g laterales (en curva) y longitudinales (frenado/aceleración).
dataguide_desc_grip_ask: Grip Ask utiliza el deslizamiento combinado nativo de la fuente cuando está disponible; para calcular el uso del círculo de fricción física se necesita el ángulo de deslizamiento físico. El deslizamiento lateral de Forza sigue siendo una relación adimensional, no grados.
dataguide_traction_grip: AGARRE — dentro del límite de adherencia (Grip Ask < 90 %)
dataguide_traction_spin: PATINAJE — superado el pico, predomina el eje longitudinal
dataguide_traction_slide: DERRAPE — superado el pico, predomina el eje lateral
dataguide_traction_lock: BLOQUEO — rueda detenida o arrastrándose al frenar
dataguide_desc_tire_temperature: Zona de temperatura superficial del neumático:
dataguide_desc_ratio: Velocidad de la rueda frente a la velocidad sobre el terreno. Un valor alto indica patinaje o bloqueo. Estado: normal <10 % · precaución <30 % · crítico por encima.
dataguide_desc_angle: Ángulo entre la orientación de la rueda y la dirección de marcha. El pico de agarre mecánico suele estar entre 6 y 12° (según la velocidad). Los umbrales disminuyen a baja velocidad.
dataguide_desc_rotation: Velocidad angular de la rueda en rad/s. Aumenta bruscamente al patinar.
dataguide_desc_wear_rate: % de neumático desgastado por segundo a la intensidad actual, medido durante la última vuelta.
dataguide_desc_load: Distribución del peso. Lon 50 % = equilibrio delante/detrás · Lat 50 % = equilibrio izquierda/derecha. Cambia al acelerar, frenar y tomar curvas.

lmu_guide_diff_coupling: In a corner, the outside wheel travels farther. More locking resists the difference in wheel speeds; it does not necessarily make them equal. Arcs show relative rotation over the same interval, not setup values.
lmu_guide_content_reference_parameters_p: Set contact-patch shape and grip. Use car-, compound- and track-specific game values, tyre temperatures and telemetry; pressures rise as tyres heat during a stint.
Above a useful range, grip may decline and slides can become less progressive
Centre of the tread overheats first; slides get snappier, less progressive
Slightly sharper initial steering response and lower rolling resistance
Balance effects depend on axle and vehicle
Open the brake ducts a step. Brake heat soaks into the rim and is often why pressures creep high
Check camber: too much inner-edge temperature drags the whole pressure up
Too little pressure can make response vague and increase shoulder loading
Tyres may take longer to reach useful temperature
Close the ducts a step to push more heat into the rims and lift pressures
Duct openings are your main in-race pressure control. Heat from the discs feeds straight into the rims
Camber decides how temperature spreads across the tread, which feeds back into pressure
Pressure changes alter tyre radius slightly, nudging ride height and rake
Track temperature and fuel burn affect tyre behaviour over a stint. Reassess using current telemetry.
lmu_guide_content_reference_parameters_c: Camber
More negative
Less negative
Tilts the top of the tyre inwards so the tread sits flat when the car rolls in a corner. You are trading mid-corner grip against straight-line braking and traction.
More mid-corner grip at that axle as the tread loads evenly under roll
Inner-edge temperature climbs; compare inner, middle and outer telemetry
Less braking and traction grip in a straight line (smaller upright contact patch)
Per axle: more front camber = sharper, slightly looser mid-corner; more rear = more planted, tighter
Re-check hot pressures. The inner edge will be doing more work
A touch less front toe-out offsets the extra scrub heat
Better braking and corner-exit traction, weaker mid-corner
Outer shoulder takes more punishment in long corners
More even wear on tracks with few fast corners
If mid-corner grip drops too far, soften the ARB at that end instead of adding camber back
Camber redistributes heat across the tread, which moves hot pressures
Caster adds dynamic camber when steered. More caster lets you run less static camber
Use inner, middle and outer tyre temperatures on the car and track in use; avoid a universal camber target.
lmu_guide_content_reference_parameters_t: Toe
More toe
Less toe
Angles the wheels relative to straight ahead. Convention: front toe-out for response, rear toe-in for stability. "More toe" here means more toe-out at the front or more toe-in at the rear.
Front toe-out: sharper, more eager turn-in. The inside wheel is already pointing into the corner
Rear toe-in: calmer, more planted corner exits and better stability over kerbs
Both add scrub. More tyre temperature, more wear, a touch more drag
Too much front toe-out makes the car nervous and darty in a straight line
Watch hot pressures rise from the extra scrub
With added rear toe-in you can often run one click less TC
Straighter-running, lower drag, cooler tyres. Good for long straights and tyre life
Lazier turn-in at the front; livelier (less damped) rear on exit
Front toe near zero suits flowing tracks; tight tracks miss the response
Add caster to recover some turn-in feel without the scrub penalty
A softer front ARB can also wake up turn-in
Toe scrub is a steady heat source. It shifts where your pressures settle
Caster and front toe both shape turn-in; tune them together
Balance shift shown is for the usual case (front response / rear stability traded together). Tune one axle at a time.
lmu_guide_content_reference_parameters_c: Caster
More
Less
Tilts the steering axis backwards. More caster gains camber as you steer. Grip arrives exactly when you wind on lock, and strengthens self-centring.
More dynamic camber mid-corner: front grip improves the more lock you carry
Heavier, more communicative steering with stronger self-centring
Slightly more stable under braking
Usually low downside. Many setups run plenty of caster for the front grip
You may be able to take out a little static camber and gain braking grip for free
Lighter steering, weaker feedback
Less camber gain. The front washes out earlier in long corners
Add static camber back to recover mid-corner front grip
Caster is camber-on-demand: the two budgets add together when steered
Caster is close to a free upgrade for front grip on cars that expose it. Lower it mainly if steering weight bothers you. Note many LMU cars list caster as non-adjustable.
lmu_guide_content_reference_parameters_r: Aero
Rear wing
More wing
Less wing

The big lever for rear downforce. Every step changes three things at once: rear grip at speed, drag, and the front-to-rear aero balance. Its effects grow with speed. It does almost nothing in a hairpin.
Rear planted in fast corners and under braking from high speed
More drag. Top speed drops, fuel use rises slightly
Aero balance moves rearwards: understeer builds the faster the corner
Car becomes less pitch-sensitive. More forgiving over crests and kerbs at speed
Lower the front (or raise the rear). More rake pulls aero balance forward again
Add a splitter step if the car has one, to match the front to the new rear
Move bias rearwards ~0.5%. The rear can now take more braking load
Soften the front ARB a click to claw back grip in the slow corners the wing can't help
Top speed up. Strong on long straights and for defending
Rear gets light in fast corners and under braking from speed
Oversteer grows with speed; the car rewards smooth hands
More pitch-sensitive: kerbs and bumps at speed unsettle it more
Move bias forward to protect the now-lighter rear under braking
Drop the rear a touch (less rake) to push aero balance back
Soften the rear ARB so mechanical grip covers some of what the aero gave up
Rake and wing together set the aero balance. Change one, re-check the other
Rear downforce decides how much braking the rear axle can take at speed
More wing means more load crushing the rear at speed. The springs must hold the platform
Front and rear aero are a matched pair; moving one strands the other
Rule of thumb: if the balance problem appears only in fast corners, it's aero. If it's everywhere, look at mechanical grip first.
lmu_guide_content_reference_parameters_f: Front splitter
More splitter
Less splitter

Adds front downforce on cars that expose a front-aero adjustment (front wing position, splitter, or front diffuser, depending on the car). The front-end counterpart to the rear wing, and like the wing, it only works at speed.
Front bites harder in fast corners. Turn-in at speed sharpens
Aero balance moves forward: the rear becomes comparatively lighter
Small drag increase
Works harder the closer the front runs to the ground
Add wing to keep the rear matched
Raise the front slightly if high-speed oversteer appears
High-speed understeer; the rear feels relatively more secure
A touch less drag
Trim a step of wing to re-centre the aero balance
Splitter and wing set the two ends of the aero see-saw
Splitter performance is very sensitive to front ride height
If your car has no splitter setting, rake (ride heights) is your front-downforce tool instead.
lmu_guide_content_reference_parameters_r: Front ride height

With the rear height, this sets rake. The nose-down angle of the floor. More rake (lower front) means more front downforce. Lower also drops the centre of gravity. The catch: run too low and the car sits on its bumpstops.
Less rake. Aero balance shifts rearwards, high-speed understeer
More suspension travel: friendlier over kerbs and bumps
Slightly higher centre of gravity
Trim a step of wing so the rear doesn't over-dominate the new balance
Raise the rear by the same amount if you only wanted clearance, not a rake change
More rake. Front downforce up, sharper at speed
Lower centre of gravity: a little less weight transfer everywhere
Risk: bottoming onto the bumpstops mid-corner causes sudden, ugly understeer over bumps and kerbs
Stiffen or shorten bumpstop range so the platform stays controlled when it touches down
Stiffer front springs help hold the car off the stops
If it's now loose at speed, a step of wing rebalances it
The lower you run, the more the bumpstops become part of the active suspension
Splitter downforce rises sharply as the front nears the ground
Springs and ride height together decide whether the floor stays where you put it
Rake and wing are the two halves of aero balance
Low-and-stiff setups lean on this: maximum rake with the bumpstops doing real work to hold the aero platform.
Rear ride height
The other half of rake. Raising the rear tips the floor nose-down (more rake, more front aero) but lifts the centre of gravity at the driven axle.
More rake. Aero balance forward, livelier at speed
Higher rear CoG: a bit more weight transfer, slightly more squat and dive
Diffuser/floor generally works the rake harder (car-dependent)
A step of wing covers the rear if high-speed confidence drops
Check rear springs. More transfer may want a touch more support
Less rake, high-speed understeer tendency
Lower CoG at the rear: traction off slow corners often improves
Less travel before the rear bumpstops
Lower the front too if you want the rake back with a lower car overall
Rake is the difference between the two heights. They only mean something together
Rake and wing trade against each other for the same aero balance
Height changes shift how soon the rear reaches its bumpstops
Tune rake in small steps. Evaluate rake on the car and track in use.
lmu_guide_content_reference_parameters_s: Suspension & dampers
Front springs
Stiffer
Softer
Wheel rate at the front. Stiffness trades slow-corner mechanical grip against response and aero platform stability.
Sharper, more immediate turn-in response
Less mechanical front grip. Understeer in slow corners
Steadier front platform: splitter and rake work more consistently at speed (can make it *looser* in fast corners)
Harsher over kerbs and bumps
Soften the front ARB to win back slow-corner grip while keeping the response
Re-match damper rates to the new spring. Stiffer springs want more damping
You can often run a little lower now the spring holds the platform
More slow-corner front grip as the tyre stays loaded over bumps
Lazier response; more dive under braking
Front aero platform moves around more. Less consistent at speed
Soften front damping to match, or the spring can't do its job
May need a touch more ride height to avoid the bumpstops
Dampers are tuned to the spring. Change one without the other and the wheel loses contact
Softer springs reach the stops sooner; stiffer springs may never use them
Spring rate decides how far the car settles and how low you can safely run
Mechanical grip rules according to the corner and platform. Decide which corners matter at this track before touching springs.
Rear springs
Wheel rate at the rear, the traction axle. The classic trade: softer rear hooks up out of slow corners, stiffer rear holds the aero platform at speed.
Less traction out of slow corners. Power oversteer appears earlier
Steadier rear platform: more consistent downforce in fast corners
Sharper response to throttle balance changes
Soften the rear ARB to recover some slow-corner traction
A click more TC papers over exit wheelspin while you test
Re-match rear damping
Better drive off slow corners. The rear squats and grips
More squat means more dynamic rake change: aero balance moves around on throttle
Slightly tighter feel overall
Soften rear damping to suit
Check the rear isn't now sitting on its bumpstops under load
Spring rate and diff locking both shape how the rear puts power down
Springs and dampers are one system
Softer rear = more squat = the static height number means something different
lmu_guide_content_reference_parameters_a: Front anti-roll bar
Resists body roll by tying the front wheels together. The cleanest mid-corner balance tool there is. It changes roll stiffness distribution without touching ride or aero.
Crisper, flatter turn-in
More load forced through the outside front, mid-corner understeer
Inside front stays more planted under braking
Stiffen the rear bar too if you wanted response, not a balance change
The loaded outside front may want a touch more camber
More mid-corner front grip. The car rotates better
Slower, softer initial response; more body roll
Can feel lazy on quick direction changes (chicanes)
Slightly firmer front slow bump keeps transitions tidy despite the softer bar
Balance lives in the front/rear bar *ratio*. One bar alone is half the story
Bars and springs both add roll stiffness; they overlap
ARBs are the first thing to reach for when the balance problem is mid-corner, at all speeds.
Rear anti-roll bar
The rear half of the roll-stiffness ratio. Strongly shapes on-throttle behaviour from mid-corner to exit.
Car rotates more. Oversteer, especially on throttle from mid-corner
Flatter, more responsive rear in direction changes
Inside rear unloads more: worse traction out of slow corners
A little more preload can steady the rear on throttle pickup
One more click of TC while you learn the new balance
More traction and a calmer rear on exit
More roll; slightly lazier in chicanes
Mild understeer tendency mid-corner
Soften the front bar too if you only wanted traction, not push
It's the ratio between bars that sets balance
Both control how the rear behaves under power
lmu_guide_content_reference_parameters_d: Dampers (bump / rebound)

Dampers don't change how much weight transfers, only how fast. Slow bump/rebound shape braking, turn-in and throttle transitions; fast bump/rebound handle kerbs and bumps. They are your transient balance tool.
Weight transfer slows down: calmer, more deliberate transitions
Stiffer front bump = less dive, lazier turn-in (entry understeer)
Stiffer rear rebound = rear held down on throttle, steadier exits
Stiffer fast damping = harsh over kerbs; the wheel can skip and lose contact
Damping should track spring rate. If you're maxing dampers, the spring is wrong
On kerb-heavy tracks, let fast damping stay soft and use bumpstops for the platform
Faster weight transfer: livelier turn-in, more dive and squat
Better kerb absorption and bumpy-track compliance
Too soft and the car floats. Balance becomes vague and delayed
If the car got too eager on entry, a stiffer front bar steadies it without slowing the dampers again
Each spring rate has a damping range that suits it
Fast damping and bumpstops share the job of kerbs and bottoming
Diagnose dampers by *when* the problem happens: entry/exit transitions = slow damping; kerbs and bumps = fast damping; steady mid-corner = not the dampers.
lmu_guide_content_reference_parameters_b: Bumpstops (rate / range)
Stiffer / less range
Softer / more range
Secondary springs that catch the suspension at the end of its travel. In a low-and-stiff setup they're not just a safety net. They become an aero-platform tool the car deliberately rides on.
Car rides the stops sooner/harder: very consistent aero platform at speed
Sudden balance change the instant one end hits. Can feel like a wall of understeer (front) or a snap (rear)
Harsh over kerbs
Tune ride height so the stops engage where you want them to, not by accident
Main spring and stop share the load. Set them as a pair
More usable travel, friendlier kerbs
Aero platform floats more at speed, less consistent downforce
Risk of harsh bottoming if you're running very low
Raise slightly if the floor is slamming down on compressions
Ride height decides when the stops engage
Total wheel rate = spring + engaged bumpstop
Fast damping and stops both manage big hits
If the balance changes *suddenly* at one speed or one compression, suspect a bumpstop engaging.
Brakes
Brake bias
Forward
Rearward

Splits braking force front/rear. The fastest balance change in the car. And the one you can adjust from the wheel mid-stint. Its effect is speed-sensitive, because at high speed the wing is pressing the rear down.
Stable, predictable braking; the rear stays in line
Front lockup risk rises, especially as the fronts wear
Understeer on corner entry under trail-braking. The car resists rotation
On LMGT3, select an ABS map suited to the car before tuning bias; map numbers are not a universal intervention scale
Softer front bar restores some entry rotation
Car rotates into the corner under trail-braking, great for hairpins
Rear lockup / snap risk under hard braking, worst at low speed where the wing isn't helping
Less margin in panic stops and on cold tyres
More wing makes rearward bias safer at speed (but not in slow corners)
On LMGT3, evaluate the chosen ABS map and rearward bias separately; increasing the map number is not a universal safety net
Rear downforce sets how much braking the rear can take. Bias and wing move together
The selected ABS map and brake bias interact; changing both together can cause instability
Off-throttle diff locking also shapes entry rotation, they stack
Tune in small increments and reassess after representative laps; no universal bias window is claimed.
Brake pressure
Higher
Sets how pedal travel reaches the calipers. Suitable pressure depends on the car, its ABS capability, tyre grip and pedal input; confirm behaviour in-game.
Higher pressure can increase braking force while tyre grip permits
Without ABS, higher pressure can increase lockup risk, especially as aerodynamic load changes through braking
Less modulation. The pedal becomes an on/off switch rather than a dial
If pressure changes, recheck front/rear balance and lock behaviour.
ABS behaviour and pressure response vary by car; verify in-game.
More modulation. A usable range under your foot instead of a cliff edge
Lower pressure can improve modulation and reduce lock risk; verify the useful level in-game
Slightly longer stops if you go too low. You are leaving clamping force on the table
On cars exposing migration, assess pressure and migration together during a stop.
Lower pressure lets you run slightly more rearward bias without the snap
ABS capability changes how pressure affects lockup
Pressure sets how hard you can brake, bias sets where. They are one system
Migration shifts bias through the stop as the wing fades; pressure decides whether the fronts survive that shift
Brake pressure depends on car capability, track, tyre state and pedal input. Treat community advice as a prompt to evaluate in-game, not a target.
Brake ducts
More open
More closed
Cooling for discs and pads. But their stealth role is tyre pressure control, because brake heat soaks through the rim into the air in the tyre.
Cooler brakes: consistent pedal, less pad wear over a stint
Tyre pressures settle lower as the rims run cooler (the exact kPa per step varies by car)
A little more drag; brakes and tyres take longer to warm up
Raise cold pressures to land in the same hot window
Faster warm-up. Good for short stints, qualifying and cold tracks
Pressures settle higher; fade and pad wear risk in long stints
Slightly less drag
Drop cold pressures to compensate for the extra rim heat
Duct steps are effectively a pressure adjustment you can plan a stint around
Brake temperature changes pedal feel and bite, which changes how a given bias behaves
Duct (and radiator) openings are one of the few "free" tools for managing temperatures and pressures without touching the rest of the setup. LMU also exposes brake duct blanking front and rear.
lmu_guide_content_reference_parameters_d: Drivetrain & electronics
Differential preload

How strongly the diff resists a speed difference between the rear wheels before torque is even applied. It shapes the car in the *transitions*. Off-throttle into the corner, and the moment you pick the throttle back up.
More locked off-throttle: stable, planted entry that resists rotation (entry understeer)
Stronger, more connected drive on throttle pickup
On tight exits the locked axle can push wide. Or snap if grip runs out
Smoother across throttle transitions overall
A touch rearward bias restores entry rotation the preload took away
Softer front bar also brings back rotation, mid-corner instead of entry
Car rotates freely off-throttle, agile, eager entries
Throttle pickup feels looser; inside wheel spins up easier out of slow corners
Can feel nervous in fast lift-off moments
A click more TC covers the looser throttle pickup
Slightly softer rear springs add traction to compensate
Both shape entry rotation. Set them as a pair
TC and the diff fight over the same wheelspin
Rear roll stiffness changes how loaded each rear wheel is, which changes what the diff sees
Test preload in the slowest corner on the track. That's where its character is loudest.
Differential power
More lock
Less lock

How hard the rear diff locks under throttle. Preload sets the baseline; power lock adds to it the harder you accelerate. Locked, the diff drives the loaded outside rear harder than the inside one, and that difference swings the car round, most noticeably in first to third gear corners. Some cars show it as a ramp angle, where a lower angle locks more.
Car rotates more on throttle: the outside rear drives it round
Inside rear stops spinning up on its own
Rear can step out as the power goes down, especially in slow corners
Strong, connected drive once the car is straight
A click more TC catches the rear if it now steps out on exit
Slightly softer rear springs help the rear hook up again
Calmer, more stable exits: the rear stays behind you
Car rotates less on throttle and can push wide on tight exits
Inside rear can spin up on its own out of slow corners
A touch more preload stops the inside wheel spinning alone
A softer front bar helps the nose keep turning on power
Preload is the baseline lock and power adds to it under throttle, so read them together
TC and the diff are both managing wheelspin, so set them as a pair
Coast shapes the entry, power the exit. Change one and re-check the other
Judge it on the exit of the slowest corner on the track. If the car swings round as you open the throttle, take lock away; if it won't turn on power and the inside wheel spins alone, add some.
Differential coast

How hard the rear diff locks off the throttle: braking, trail-braking and turn-in. More lock ties the rear wheels together and keeps the rear planted; less lets the car rotate into the corner. Some cars show it as a ramp angle, where a lower angle locks more.
Stable, planted rear under braking and turn-in
Resists rotation on entry and can bring entry understeer
Calmer over kerbs and bumps off the throttle
A touch of rearward bias gives back some entry rotation
A softer front bar helps the nose turn in
Car rotates more freely into the corner
Rear can get nervous or snap under trail-braking
Rewards a smooth release of the brake
Move bias forward a touch if the rear gets nervous under braking
On Hypercars, migration can steady the rear as you trail off the brake
Both shape how the car rotates on entry, so set them as a pair
Preload is the baseline and coast lock adds to it off the throttle
Coast shapes the entry, power the exit
Test it in a slow corner with a long braking zone. That is where coast lock shows most.
lmu_guide_content_reference_parameters_e: Traction control manages wheelspin through slip threshold, power cut and lateral slip-angle settings. Native ABS is limited to LMGT3; its maps tune particular behaviours, not a universal more/less intervention scale. Car electronics and optional driving assists are distinct.
Earlier or stronger TC intervention can make exits more repeatable
Excessive TC power cut can cost exit speed
Slip threshold, power cut and lateral slip target change different aspects of intervention
Check the actual car's response rather than assuming all settings increase intervention in the same direction
If you keep needing more TC, the real fix is often diff/springs at the rear
Less TC intervention exposes more of the car's traction behaviour
Wheelspin can punish abrupt throttle inputs
Sliding can increase tyre wear; assess telemetry and representative laps
Softer rear springs / ARB make low TC liveable
A touch more rear toe-in steadies exits without electronic help
Diff locking and TC manage the same exit wheelspin from opposite ends
Choose a suitable LMGT3 ABS map before tuning brake bias; no universal numeric map direction is established
Wheelspin and sliding can increase tyre temperature; TC settings alter when and how power is cut
Evaluate TC slip threshold, power cut and slip angle separately. For LMGT3 ABS, use the official map diagram and in-game behaviour instead of treating a higher map number as more assistance.
lmu_guide_content_reference_parameters_v: Virtual Energy is an allocation control where present. Its presence does not prove a car is hybrid; plan using the game display and measured consumption.
Larger permitted energy use per stint, provided the fuel load covers the plan
The chosen NRG allocation affects pit-stop duration; it is not battery charge
Fuel carried and energy allowance must both cover measured consumption
Plan fuel carried against the chosen NRG allowance; extra fuel adds weight without increasing that allowance
Smaller permitted energy use per stint; fuel weight depends on fuel carried, not NRG alone
Less margin before exhausting the allowance and incurring a penalty
Use measured consumption, lift-and-coast and short shifting to conserve energy
Match Fuel Ratio to the energy you actually carry so the two agree
Energy and fuel are two views of the same stint plan, set them together
Harvest restores hybrid battery charge, not the Virtual Energy stint allowance
Virtual Energy may be present outside hybrid cars; do not infer hybrid capability from its presence.
lmu_guide_content_reference_parameters_f: Fuel Ratio
Richer / more
Leaner / less
Fuel control meaning varies by car. Use in-game displayed fuel and measured consumption to plan a stint.
More litres on board: longer stint, more early-stint weight
Heavier car blunts traction and braking slightly until it burns down
Useful to cover an extra lap if strategy is marginal
Use the displayed fuel and energy values to plan the stint.
Lighter, faster car, qualifying trim
Shorter stint; risk of running dry if you misjudge consumption
The car comes alive as fuel burns off regardless. Plan for the lap-1 weight
A heavy fuel load shifts weight rearward slightly. You may want a touch more front bias early
Litres and energy allocation describe the same stint, they must agree
Always plan fuel from a real consumption figure (the in-game MFD or a test stint), not a guess.
lmu_guide_content_reference_parameters_r: Regen level
More harvest
Less harvest

On a confirmed hybrid, regeneration converts braking energy into battery charge. Battery charge is separate from the Virtual Energy stint allowance. Axle and scale are car-specific; assess in-game response rather than assuming common values.
Refills the battery faster, supporting continued deployment; it does not refill the NRG allowance
Adds engine/MGU braking at the harvest axle: can tug the balance under braking
On front-axle-harvest cars, strong regen can nudge the nose into the corner
Heat and wear into the harvest-axle tyres rise slightly
Re-check brake bias. Regen braking stacks on top of the friction brakes at that axle
A stronger deploy map spends what the harvest brings in, balance the two
Cleaner, more neutral braking feel. Fewer hybrid effects on entry
Less battery charge recovered; balance deployment and harvest while monitoring fuel and NRG separately
Easier to drive consistently if the harvest braking was unsettling you
Monitor the NRG allowance independently; carrying more NRG does not restore battery charge
Harvest fills the battery, the deploy map empties it. Set them as a pair
Regen braking changes the effective bias at the harvest axle
Regeneration replenishes battery charge, while NRG tracks the permitted combined energy use per stint
Step sizes for regen vary by car (the scale is car-specific). Use the displayed in-game value; do not assume a shared scale.
lmu_guide_content_reference_parameters_m: On hybrid Hypercars, the electric motor map controls battery deployment. The MGU replaces ICE torque under the combined power limit; it does not add extra total power. LMDh deploys through the rear axle; front-hybrid LMH deploys through the front axle above its permitted deployment speed.
More battery deployment replaces a larger share of ICE torque; it does not increase combined power
Battery charge is spent faster; balance deployment with harvest and monitor the state of charge
Fuel consumption can fall as electric torque replaces combustion-engine torque
Axle torque distribution and handling depend on the car and permitted deployment speed
Lift harvest to keep up with the faster drain
Reassess traction-control behaviour on the actual car when deployment changes axle torque distribution
Less battery deployment leaves more of the required output to the combustion engine
Battery charge is spent more slowly; reduced deployment is not a universal slower-exit rule
Less electric contribution can increase fuel consumption; check fuel and battery separately
Balance harvest with deployment while leaving battery capacity available for regeneration
Deploy and harvest are the two halves of the energy loop
NRG limits combined energy use per stint; battery charge is a separate budget, not an extra NRG allocation
Official LMU guidance describes deployment as fuel-efficiency management, not an extra-power boost. Read the car's displayed map and battery charge; no universal SVM click scale is established.
lmu_guide_content_reference_parameters_f: Front differential (Hypercar)

Front-drive-axle Hypercars expose a front diff (power, coast and preload) on top of the rear. It shapes how the front axle puts down hybrid/engine torque and how it behaves trailing off the throttle. A handling tool the GT3s and LMPs don't have.
More front-axle locking: steadier front under power on deploy, but more understeer as both front wheels tie together
Coast side: more locking calms the front entering a corked off-throttle
Can mask front mechanical grip problems rather than fix them
Soften the front ARB to recover the mid-corner rotation the lock takes away
Front deploy and front diff interact. Re-check exit feel after changing either
Freer front axle: more rotation, livelier turn-in, but more torque-steer/instability under front deploy
Less predictable on bumpy front-axle exits
Rewards smooth throttle on the way out
A click more TC steadies things while you test a freer front diff
Front and rear diff behaviour combine into the overall on/off-throttle balance
On front-deploy cars, the diff decides how that power axle behaves

Front-hybrid LMH cars (Ferrari 499P, Toyota GR010/TR010, Peugeot 9X8 and Isotta Tipo 6) drive through the front axle. LMDh and non-hybrid LMH cars do not. Check the setup's capability badge and field lock reason; a dummy front-diff value does not prove front-wheel drive.
lmu_guide_content_reference_parameters_b: Brake migration
More migration
Less migration

Shifts brake bias forward as you bleed off the pedal through a braking zone. More front bias on initial hard braking, migrating rearward as you trail off. Lets you run a stable-on-initial, rotational-on-release brake feel that a single fixed bias can't.
More forward bias at the top of the brake zone: stable, lock-resistant initial braking
As you trail off, bias moves rearward. Helps the car rotate towards the apex
Too much can make the rear feel like it wakes up unexpectedly mid-release
Set your base bias first, then add migration for the trail-braking phase
Bias stays closer to fixed through the zone, simpler, more predictable
Less help rotating the car on brake release
Better if migration was making the rear nervous
Without migration you may want a touch less base front bias for entry rotation
Migration moves *around* your base bias, they're set together
ABS changes how much migration you can run before the rear locks

A little migration goes a long way. Add it in single clicks and feel the brake-release phase specifically. On a hybrid car, remember regen is also braking at the driven axle, so the two stack: LMDh regen adds rear effort, front-hybrid LMH regen adds front.
lmu_guide_content_reference_parameters_t: 3rd spring / heave (Hypercar/LMP)

A central heave element that resists both wheels compressing together (pure vertical / aero load) without affecting roll. Prototypes use it to hold the aero platform under high downforce while keeping the corner springs soft for mechanical grip. The corner springs and the 3rd spring are set independently. The 3rd is not L/R linked.
Holds ride height better under aero load at speed, more consistent downforce
Less dive/squat from pure vertical loads (braking, crests) without stiffening roll
Too stiff and the platform stops absorbing big vertical hits, skittish over crests
You can often keep the corner springs softer for mechanical grip, letting the 3rd hold the platform
3rd spring and packers both manage end-of-travel, set them together
More compliant over big vertical inputs. Better mechanical grip on bumps and crests
Platform moves more at speed: aero height varies more through a fast corner
May reach the packers/bumpstops sooner under heavy aero load
Check the car isn't dropping onto its bumpstops at speed with a softer heave
Corner springs handle roll + heave together; the 3rd spring handles heave only. They overlap on vertical loads
Both manage how the platform behaves at the end of vertical travel
Heave stiffness changes how low the car runs dynamically at speed

GT3s generally have no active 3rd spring (it reads N/A); it is primarily a prototype tool. View / Edit shows fields present in the setup and keeps third-element settings independent from corner linking.
lmu_guide_content_reference_symptoms_ent: Corner entry
Won't turn in (entry understeer)
You brake, turn, and the nose washes wide before the apex. Worst while you're still on the brakes.
Cheapest test first: move brake bias a small amount rearward from the wheel. If it improves, the problem is your entry tools, not outright front grip.
Bias too far forward
Move rearward in 0.5% steps. Frees the car to rotate under trail-braking
Diff preload too high
Lower it. A locked diff resists rotation off-throttle
Front slow bump too stiff
Soften so the nose can dive and load the fronts on turn-in
Front bar too stiff
Soften a click. This helps mid-corner too
Fronts out of the window
Check hot pressures before touching anything mechanical
Rear snaps under trail-braking
The rear steps out as you brake and turn in together, the classic spin-at-corner-entry.
Note where it happens. Fast corners point to aero; slow corners point to bias, diff or cold rears.
Bias too far rearward
Test a small forward bias change for stability
Regen too high (LMDh)
On an LMDh, harvest is rear braking the bias slider doesn't show. A click less regen calms the rear on entry. Not a factor on non-hybrid cars
Preload too low
More preload steadies the rear off-throttle
Not enough rear downforce (fast corners only)
Add a step of wing if it only happens at speed
Cold or low rear pressures
Rears below the window can't take braking and turning at once
Rear rebound too stiff
Soften so the rear stays planted as weight moves forward
lmu_guide_content_reference_symptoms_mid: The front washes out at steady throttle, slow and fast corners alike. A mechanical front grip shortage.
"All speeds" is the key clue. If it were only fast corners, it would be aero. See the high-speed symptoms instead.
Soften. The cleanest mid-corner balance tool there is
More negative camber; check inner temps afterwards
Soften for slow-corner grip (costs a little response)
High pressures shrink the contact patch
The rear edges wide at steady state and you're constantly making small corrections.
Same logic in reverse: everywhere = mechanical, fast corners only = aero.
More negative rear camber plants the rear mid-corner
A touch more calms the rear everywhere
lmu_guide_content_reference_symptoms_fas: High-speed corners
Understeer only in fast corners
Fine in the slow stuff, but the nose pushes in quick corners. An aero balance problem.
Confirm it really is speed-dependent before touching aero. One slow corner with push disqualifies this diagnosis.
Not enough rake
Lower the front (or raise the rear) to pull aero balance forward
Splitter setting too low
Add a step if your car has one
Too much wing
Trim a step. You gain top speed as a bonus
Nervous or loose at high speed
No confidence in fast corners; the rear feels light over crests and quick direction changes.
If the balance changes suddenly at one specific compression, suspect a bumpstop engaging rather than pure aero.
Not enough wing
Add a step. The single biggest fix for this
Too much rake
Lower the rear a touch
Rear riding its stops
More range or softer rate at the rear

What is Virtual Energy? (NRG)
Regeneration and battery charge
Regenerative braking converts braking energy into battery charge. Battery charge and the Virtual Energy stint allowance are separate quantities.
LMDh uses a rear-axle MGU; hybrid LMH usually uses a front-axle MGU.
A fully charged battery cannot accept regeneration, increasing reliance on friction brakes and their temperatures.
Balance harvest and deployment during the stint. Regeneration refills the battery, not the NRG allowance.
Virtual Energy is a stint allowance
Virtual Energy (NRG) limits combined energy consumption per stint. It is not the hybrid battery's state of charge, and its presence does not establish hybrid capability.
LMGT3 and non-hybrid LMH also use NRG, based on their fuel consumption.
The selected NRG allocation affects pit-stop duration. Monitor the remaining allowance separately from fuel and battery charge.
The reviewed guide specifies a 100-second stop-and-go when NRG reaches zero, with harsher penalties for repeated violations.
Lift-and-coast and short shifting are documented energy-saving techniques.
Fuel carried versus energy allowance
Fuel Ratio determines fuel carried relative to the NRG stint allowance. Carrying extra fuel does not increase that allowance.
Plan fuel and NRG from measured consumption and the in-car displays, rather than confusing either with battery charge.
Hybrid deployment can reduce fuel consumption without increasing combined power output.
Avoid unnecessary fuel weight; preserve enough battery charge for hybrid operation, including LMDh pit-lane power.
Native ABS and car-specific maps
LMGT3 is the only category with native ABS. Other classes may use a separate driving assist; that is not evidence of native ABS capability.
Since the June 2025 refinement, ABS maps tune particular behaviours rather than representing a simple progression from less to more intervention.
Choose a suitable ABS map before adjusting brake bias; changing the two together can cause instability.
Use the official car-map diagram and in-game behaviour, not an assumed universal one-click ABS direction.
ABS (Anti-Lock Braking System) for LMGT3 Cars
Three traction-control settings
LMU traction control is managed by the car, not an additional driving assist. Its settings control different aspects of intervention.
Traction Control sets the slip allowed before intervention; Power Cut sets how much power is removed; Slip Angle targets lateral slip before activation.
These controls can be adjusted in the garage's powertrain menu and on track through the MFD electronics menu.
Electric motor map can change the axle torque distribution; assess the actual car rather than assuming one generic TC setting covers every effect.
